hero.headline: Fort Pierce commission votes 3-2 to give King's Landing developer six more months to raise $15 million
hero.teaser: Fort Pierce city commissioners voted 3-2 Monday night to give the developer of King's Landing another six months to secure the additional $15 million it says it needs to build a pl
hero.body:
Fort Pierce city commissioners voted 3-2 Monday night to give the developer of King's Landing another six months to secure the additional $15 million it says it needs to build a planned $65 million Marriott hotel. The decision followed a lengthy debate over whether to continue working with developer Live Oak or terminate the agreement.

 Live Oak is planning the Marriott hotel as part of the $200 million King's Landing development along the city's waterfront. Joe Collier, a hotel operating and hospitality partner, told commissioners the team will use a different approach to raising the money and needs additional time to put that plan into action. The developer has already missed a key deadline under its agreement with the city.

 Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky pushed for termination, calling the missed deadline a material breach. Commissioner Michael Broderick argued that ending the agreement could create even more delays. Broderick said pulling the plug now could mean 10 years of turnaround time before anything is completed. He called the project integrally critical to Fort Pierce and said the city needs a downtown hotel and more downtown retail.

 Community members were divided on the extension. Howard Dunn Jr. told commissioners it was time to kick the developer to the curb and move on. Jamie Hurst said six months is not that long and urged commissioners to listen to what the developer has to say. Fort Pierce resident Charlie Hagg said the community would be delighted to have a Marriott downtown.

 A new agreement will be drafted over the next 30 days. Live Oak will then have six months to secure the additional funding needed for the hotel. If the project stays on track, city leaders say construction could begin in roughly one to one-and-a-half years. The planned project is expected to bring millions of dollars in economic activity to the area.

cards.headline: Detainees held in 18-square-foot metal enclosures at Alligator Alcatraz, DHS finds
cards.teaser: A federal inspector general report documented 79 detainees confined in small metal enclosures at Florida's now-closed Everglades detention center, while the state has received only $84.5 million of an expected $608 million in federal reimbursement.
cards.body:
A Department of Homeland Security inspector general report found that 79 detainees were confined in metal enclosures offering about 18 square feet of floor space at Florida's now-closed Everglades immigration detention center known as Alligator Alcatraz, with stays ranging from several minutes to nearly two hours. The findings from an unannounced January inspection documented serious health and safety failures at the facility, which ceased operating in June, while Gov. Ron DeSantis defended the operation Monday and said Florida's detention assistance helped federal authorities detain and deport about 25,000 people.

 The confinement practice occurred between July 17, 2025, and January, with detainees exposed to outdoor temperatures in the small enclosures. Inspectors described the practice as unprecedented among detention facilities their office had inspected and a significant risk to detainees' health and safety. Staff described the spaces as calming areas for people seeking time alone, though inspectors also identified an instance in which an enclosure was used after a detainee failed to follow a command.

 The federal review documented additional failures including insects in bathing areas, showers limited to three times a week, and inadequate recreation. Inspectors also found shortcomings in medical care and food service, while finding compliance in the intake and use-of-force areas they reviewed. Staff could not consistently identify which detention standards applied, according to the report. The inspector general administratively closed all 10 recommendations because the facility had ceased operating.

 Speaking in Lakeland on Monday, DeSantis said the goal had been to exceed federal standards and argued that Florida's assistance was necessary to help carry out the Trump administration's deportation plans. He acknowledged he had not read the report. His remarks referred to both Alligator Alcatraz and a Baker County operation, and DeSantis said the federal government had approved reimbursement for the state's work.

 The findings emerge amid a continued fight over emergency powers and public money used to run the facility. The Florida Division of Emergency Management submitted its overdue spending report Friday, and lawmakers approved another $250 million for emergency expenses, including immigration costs. That report showed Florida had received $84.5 million of an expected $608 million in federal reimbursement for detention centers and listed more than $417 million in unpaid immigration-related invoices as of June 30.

 Schedules and admission details can change, so check the individual event page before heading out.

 1. Marine Flea Market and Boat Sale — Port St. Lucie

 Saturday, Sept. 19, 9 a.m.-5 p.m. | MIDFLORIDA Event Center, 9221 SE Event Center Place

The event listing advertises new and used boats, fishing seminars and workshops, U.S. Coast Guard participation, seafood, beach music, marine bargains and closeout fishing and boating gear.

 View the Marine Flea Market and Boat Sale event page .

 View the Bullfrogs & Butterflies Family Barn Dance event page .

 3. Joe Reid & Heartland Band — Vero Beach

 Saturday, Sept. 19, 5:30-8:30 p.m. | Riverside Theatre, 3250 Riverside Park Drive 

 For a Saturday evening music option in Indian River County, Riverside Theatre has Joe Reid & Heartland Band on its calendar for a three-hour country performance.

 View the Joe Reid & Heartland Band event page .

 4. Rock'n Riverwalk — Stuart

 Sunday, Sept. 20, 1-4 p.m. | Riverwalk Stage, 121 SW Flagler Avenue 

 Rock'n Riverwalk returns Sunday afternoon at the Riverwalk Stage in downtown Stuart. The City of Stuart calendar lists the live-music event from 1 to 4 p.m., making it an easy daytime option before the weekend winds down.

 View the Rock'n Riverwalk event page .

 5. The Artimus Pyle Band — Stuart

 Sunday, Sept. 20, 7 p.m. | The Lyric Theatre, 59 SW Flagler Avenue | $60 

 The Lyric Theatre closes out the weekend with The Artimus Pyle Band, honoring Ronnie Van Zant's Lynyrd Skynyrd. The event listing describes Pyle as the last surviving member and drummer of the classic Lynyrd Skynyrd lineup and notes his 2006 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction with the band.

hero.headline: Detainees held in 18-square-foot metal enclosures at Alligator Alcatraz, DHS finds
hero.teaser: A federal inspector general report documented 79 detainees confined in small metal enclosures at Florida's now-closed Everglades detention center, while the state has received only $84.5 million of an expected $608 million in federal reimbursement.
hero.body:
A Department of Homeland Security inspector general report found that 79 detainees were confined in metal enclosures offering about 18 square feet of floor space at Florida's now-closed Everglades immigration detention center known as Alligator Alcatraz, with stays ranging from several minutes to nearly two hours. The findings from an unannounced January inspection documented serious health and safety failures at the facility, which ceased operating in June, while Gov. Ron DeSantis defended the operation Monday and said Florida's detention assistance helped federal authorities detain and deport about 25,000 people.

 The confinement practice occurred between July 17, 2025, and January, with detainees exposed to outdoor temperatures in the small enclosures. Inspectors described the practice as unprecedented among detention facilities their office had inspected and a significant risk to detainees' health and safety. Staff described the spaces as calming areas for people seeking time alone, though inspectors also identified an instance in which an enclosure was used after a detainee failed to follow a command.

 The federal review documented additional failures including insects in bathing areas, showers limited to three times a week, and inadequate recreation. Inspectors also found shortcomings in medical care and food service, while finding compliance in the intake and use-of-force areas they reviewed. Staff could not consistently identify which detention standards applied, according to the report. The inspector general administratively closed all 10 recommendations because the facility had ceased operating.

 Speaking in Lakeland on Monday, DeSantis said the goal had been to exceed federal standards and argued that Florida's assistance was necessary to help carry out the Trump administration's deportation plans. He acknowledged he had not read the report. His remarks referred to both Alligator Alcatraz and a Baker County operation, and DeSantis said the federal government had approved reimbursement for the state's work.

 The findings emerge amid a continued fight over emergency powers and public money used to run the facility. The Florida Division of Emergency Management submitted its overdue spending report Friday, and lawmakers approved another $250 million for emergency expenses, including immigration costs. That report showed Florida had received $84.5 million of an expected $608 million in federal reimbursement for detention centers and listed more than $417 million in unpaid immigration-related invoices as of June 30.
